title: Lior and the Wardrobe
premise: Silas Reyes, a bridge inspector who measures everything and feels nothing, drifts through his marriage to Ada like a tenant until his mother-in-law's funeral, where a stranger calls the family by an old name—Vasquez—that no one uses. The stranger leaves behind a wardrobe containing letters in their mother's hand, written in a coded language she invented during her years as a translator, hinting at money, a hidden sibling, and a betrayal that bought the family its quiet life. As Silas and Ada decode the letters together—the first project they've ever shared—they discover Ada's brother was erased from memory after exposing their father's corruption, and that the stranger is his daughter. The novel ends with Silas choosing to be an owner of his life: he confronts the family's buried history publicly, reconciles with the niece he never knew, and finally speaks to Ada in the untranslatable sentence her mother left them—a sentence about staying, not leaving.
about_author: Wren Joubert spent a decade as a structural engineer before abandoning blueprints for sentences, and still cannot look at a bridge without calculating its grief. They live in a coastal town where fog does most of the talking, and this is their second novel.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Silas inspects a failing bridge while narrating his marriage in engineering terms—stress fractures, load tolerances—and admits he and Ada haven't truly spoken in years. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: numbness mistaken for peace, the reader sensing collapse long before either spouse does.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: At Marisol's funeral, a woman named Ines Vasquez approaches the family and uses a surname Silas has never heard Ada say. Ada goes white; her sister Deni pretends not to hear. POV: alternating Silas and Ada. Emotional beat: the first crack—grief interrupted by a question neither can ask aloud.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Kept
chapters.summary: Clearing the house, they find a locked wardrobe Marisol never let anyone open. Inside: bundles of letters in her invented cipher, a child's photograph with one face scratched out, and a deed to land Silas didn't know existed. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: vertigo—the mother she mourned becomes a stranger mid-mourning.

chapters.title: Cipher
chapters.summary: Silas treats the code as an engineering problem, mapping symbol frequencies on graph paper late at night. For the first time in years, he and Ada sit at the same table working toward something. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: cautious tenderness disguised as methodology; they decode only a fragment—'the money was never ours.'

chapters.title: Ines Returns
chapters.summary: Ines appears at their door claiming to be the daughter of Rafael Vasquez—Ada's brother, erased from every family story. She says Marisol wrote the letters to him, unsent, for thirty years. Deni demands she leave. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: found family knocking on the door of a family built on forgetting.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Wasn't
chapters.summary: Decoded letters reveal Rafael exposed their father's embezzlement of union pension funds; the father chose the money, the mother chose silence, and Rafael vanished. Ada realizes her entire childhood was curated. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: rage at the dead, and the terrifying freedom of no longer trusting the past.

chapters.title: Load Test
chapters.summary: Silas, decoding alone, finds a letter naming him—not by accident; Marisol vetted him before Ada married him, and approved. He also finds evidence the pension money seeded the family business Deni now runs. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: shame and resolve—he has been a tenant in someone else's cover-up without knowing it.

chapters.title: Deni's Ledger
chapters.summary: Silas brings the evidence to Deni, expecting denial; instead she confesses she found the letters years ago and chose the family's comfort over truth. The sisters fracture. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: climax of the corruption theme—power corrupting even through inheritance and love.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: The final letter decodes into a single sentence Marisol called untranslatable: 'Quedarse es también elegir'—to stay is also a choice. At the ruined family house, Silas, Ada, Deni, and Ines read it aloud together. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: catharsis; the sentence lands as both accusation and absolution.

chapters.title: Owner
chapters.summary: Months later: the pension restitution is filed, Ines is at Sunday dinner, and Silas signs papers—not for a house, but for a life he intends to keep. He tells Ada the sentence in his own words, and she answers. POV: Silas closing, Ada's voice in the last lines. Emotional beat: resolution—memory preserved imperfectly, family rebuilt wider than blood, marriage owned at last.
